claims.text: Nanoscale engineered interfaces in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Blocking dislocation motion at multilayer interfaces reduces time-dependent plastic deformation.
Multilayer interfaces pin dislocations and cause localized dislocation accumulation or pile-ups.
As-deposited HEA multilayer coatings typically have unoptimized interface spacing.
Controlled sputter deposition can vary interface spacing, layer thickness, and composition to produce distinct nanoscale interfaces.
Dislocation processes dominate plastic deformation of the proposed coatings under static or dynamic loading at approximately 298–573 K.
Dislocation pinning and pile-ups at engineered interfaces increase the effective activation energy for creep.
Increasing the obstruction of dislocation motion slows creep relative to a coating with less effective interfaces.
Optimized HEA multilayer coatings will have a lower creep strain rate than monolithic or unoptimized multilayer baselines.
Optimized HEA multilayer coatings will have a higher apparent activation energy for creep than the baseline.
Microstructural analysis of optimized coatings will reveal dislocation accumulation at multilayer interfaces.
Dislocation motion is less hindered in monolithic HEA coatings or multilayers with non-optimized interface spacing.
The proposed interface-controlled mechanism is applicable from approximately 298 to 573 K in physically vapor-deposited coatings.
Applicability outside the stated temperature range or to other deposition techniques remains unestablished.
Related HEA systems exhibit elevated-temperature deformation involving dislocation glide or dislocation creep and interfaces or hard phases that impede dislocation activity.
The magnitude of creep-resistance improvement and its sensitivity to interface spacing and chemistry are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or activation-energy increase, or failure to observe enhanced interfacial pile-ups, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
